source.name: ASTRA chemistry practice set
source.license: Original syllabus-based practice questions (exam-frequent themes; not verbatim past papers)

questions.stem: Members of one homologous series typically differ from the next by a
questions.explanation: Adjacent homologues differ by a methylene (CH2) group.

questions.stem: Open-chain organic compounds that contain no rings are described as
questions.explanation: Acyclic compounds have an open carbon skeleton with no carbocyclic ring.

questions.stem: Cyclobutane is grouped among organic compounds that are
questions.explanation: Cycloalkanes have a saturated ring and are classed as alicyclic.

questions.stem: Benzene and its typical substitution products are classified as
questions.explanation: Benzene has a cyclic conjugated pi system and is the parent arene.

questions.stem: Saturated open-chain hydrocarbons are represented by the general formula
questions.explanation: Alkanes are saturated and acyclic, so the hydrogen count is CnH2n+2.

questions.stem: Going from one homologue to the next raises the molecular mass by about
questions.explanation: A CH2 increment contributes 12 + 2 = 14 mass units.

questions.stem: Members of a homologous series are expected to show similar
questions.explanation: The same functional group gives similar chemistry; physical properties change gradually.

questions.stem: Hydrocarbons whose carbon atoms form an open chain with only single bonds are
questions.explanation: Open-chain saturated hydrocarbons are alkanes.

questions.stem: Which of the following hydrocarbons is alicyclic?
questions.explanation: Cyclohexane has a saturated ring; hexane is acyclic and benzene is aromatic.

questions.stem: Naphthalene is best placed in which structural class?
questions.explanation: Naphthalene consists of fused benzene rings and is aromatic.

questions.stem: Open-chain hydrocarbons that contain one carbon-carbon double bond follow
questions.explanation: Monoalkenes have the general formula CnH2n.

questions.stem: Ethanol and propan-1-ol belong to the same homologous series because they
options: have the same functional group and differ by CH2
are both gases at room temperature
questions.explanation: Alcohols share the hydroxy group and successive members differ by CH2.

questions.stem: The molecular formula C6H12 may belong to an alkene or a cycloalkane because both families
questions.explanation: Both monoalkenes and cycloalkanes are CnH2n, so the formula alone does not distinguish them.

questions.stem: Which pair are successive homologues?
questions.explanation: Methanol and ethanol are consecutive alcohols differing by CH2.

questions.stem: Alicyclic compounds differ from aromatic compounds in that alicyclic rings
questions.explanation: Alicyclic rings may be saturated or unsaturated but do not have aromatic delocalisation like benzene.

questions.stem: Which statement is not a general feature of a homologous series?
options: All members have the same molecular mass
questions.explanation: Molecular mass increases down the series; it is not the same for every member.

questions.stem: A hydrocarbon C4H6 is not a monoalkene. It can still be acyclic if it contains
questions.explanation: Alkynes (and dienes) can have formula CnH2n-2; C4H6 fits an acyclic alkyne such as butyne.

questions.stem: Among methane, cyclopropane and toluene, toluene is aromatic because it
options: has a benzene ring with a methyl substituent
questions.explanation: Toluene is methylbenzene; cyclopropane is alicyclic and methane is acyclic.

questions.stem: Alcohols are characterised by the presence of the
questions.explanation: The alcoholic functional group is —OH attached to an alkyl carbon.

questions.stem: An aldehyde is recognised by the formyl group written as
questions.explanation: The —CHO group is the aldehyde (formyl) function.

questions.stem: Carboxylic acids are identified in a condensed formula by the unit
questions.explanation: The carboxyl group —COOH is the acid function in organic chemistry.

questions.stem: Primary amines carry the nitrogenous group
questions.explanation: A primary amine has —NH2 attached to a carbon chain.

questions.stem: The cyano (nitrile) group is represented as
questions.explanation: Nitriles contain the —C≡N (cyano) group.

questions.stem: A nitroalkane contains the nitrogen-oxygen group
questions.explanation: The nitro functional group is —NO2.

questions.stem: A ketone is distinguished from an aldehyde because the carbonyl carbon is bonded to
questions.explanation: In a ketone the C=O carbon is attached to two carbon atoms; an aldehyde has at least one hydrogen.

questions.stem: An ether linkage consists of
options: an oxygen bridge between two carbon atoms
questions.explanation: Ethers have the R—O—R' grouping.

questions.stem: Esters are recognised by the grouping
questions.explanation: An ester has a carbonyl attached to an alkoxy group, written —COOR.

questions.stem: The amide functional group contains
questions.explanation: Amides have —CONH2 or a substituted —CONR2 unit.

questions.stem: The compound CH3COCH3 belongs to which class of carbonyl compounds?
questions.explanation: Acetone has a carbonyl carbon bonded to two methyl groups, so it is a ketone.

questions.stem: CH3CH2CN is classified as a
questions.explanation: The —CN group makes the molecule a nitrile (propanenitrile).

questions.stem: Phenol differs from an aliphatic alcohol in that the —OH is attached to
questions.explanation: In phenol the hydroxy group is bonded directly to a benzene ring.

questions.stem: In CH3COOCH3 the oxygen-containing function present is that of an
questions.explanation: Methyl ethanoate has the —COOCH3 ester grouping, not a free carboxyl or a simple ether.

questions.stem: Both ethanol and dimethyl ether have the formula C2H6O; they differ in
questions.explanation: C2H6O is an alcohol in ethanol and an ether in CH3OCH3 — functional isomers.

questions.stem: Which condensed formula contains both a carboxylic acid group and an amino group?
questions.explanation: Aminoethanoic acid (glycine) has —NH2 and —COOH on the same molecule; CH3CONH2 is an amide.

questions.stem: The unbranched four-carbon saturated hydrocarbon is named
questions.explanation: A straight chain of four carbons is butane.

questions.stem: The branched alkane (CH3)3CH is named
questions.explanation: The longest chain has three carbons with a methyl on carbon 2, so the name is 2-methylpropane.

questions.stem: While assigning an alkane name, the parent is chosen as the
questions.explanation: IUPAC alkane names use the longest continuous carbon chain as the parent.

questions.stem: The numeral 3 in 3-ethylhexane locates the
questions.explanation: The locant 3 is the carbon of the hexane chain that bears the ethyl group.

questions.stem: In pent-2-ene the '2' indicates that the
questions.explanation: Alkene locants give the lowest number to the first carbon of the C=C bond.

questions.stem: Substitutive names of ketones end with the suffix
questions.explanation: The characteristic suffix for a ketone is -one.

questions.stem: Propan-2-ol carries the hydroxy group at
questions.explanation: The locant 2 in propan-2-ol is the carbon that bears —OH.

questions.stem: The aldehyde CH3CH2CHO is named
questions.explanation: A three-carbon chain with —CHO at the end is propanal.

questions.stem: IUPAC renaming of acetic acid gives
questions.explanation: Acetic acid is the two-carbon carboxylic acid, ethanoic acid.

questions.stem: The prefix 2-methyl in 2-methylpropane means that a methyl group is
options: attached to carbon 2 of a three-carbon parent
questions.explanation: The parent is propane; a methyl branch sits on carbon 2.

questions.stem: Under IUPAC, CH2=CH2 is named
questions.explanation: The systematic name of the two-carbon alkene is ethene.

questions.stem: The three-carbon alkyne CH3C≡CH receives the name
questions.explanation: A three-carbon chain with a triple bond is propyne.

questions.stem: In 2-bromobutane the halogen is cited as a
questions.explanation: Haloalkanes are named with bromo-, chloro- etc. as prefixes on the alkane parent.

questions.stem: Dimethyl ether is given the substitutive name
questions.explanation: CH3OCH3 is methoxymethane (or methoxymethane as the alkoxyalkane name).

questions.stem: CH3CH2CH(CH3)2 should be named
questions.explanation: The longest chain has four carbons with a methyl on carbon 2, giving 2-methylbutane.

questions.stem: Numbering of a monosubstituted alkane begins from the end that
options: gives the substituent the highest locant
questions.explanation: The chain is numbered so the substituent gets the lowest possible number.

questions.stem: The two-carbon alcohol CH3CH2OH is named
questions.explanation: A two-carbon chain with —OH is ethanol.

questions.stem: The name 3-methylbutane is incorrect for (CH3)2CHCH2CH3 because numbering should give the methyl the locant
questions.explanation: Numbered from the nearer end, the branch is at carbon 2, so the name is 2-methylbutane.

questions.stem: CH3CH=CHCH3 is named as a butene with the double bond beginning at carbon
questions.explanation: The lowest set of locants for the C=C is 2, so the name is but-2-ene.

questions.stem: The hydrocarbon once called neopentane is systematically named
questions.explanation: The longest chain is three carbons with two methyl groups on carbon 2: 2,2-dimethylpropane.

questions.stem: The rejected name 2-ethylpropane actually describes the same molecule as
questions.explanation: Taking the longest chain of four carbons with a methyl branch gives 2-methylbutane, not a propane parent.

questions.stem: Between 4-methylpent-1-ene and 2-methylpent-4-ene, IUPAC prefers
questions.explanation: The double bond must receive the lowest locant, so numbering from the =CH2 end gives pent-1-ene with a 4-methyl branch.

questions.stem: The unsaturated alcohol CH2=CHCH2OH is named
questions.explanation: A three-carbon chain with a double bond and a terminal —OH is prop-2-en-1-ol (allyl alcohol).

questions.stem: For CH3CH2CH(CH3)CH2CH2CH3 the longest chain has six carbons, so the name is
questions.explanation: A six-carbon parent with a methyl at carbon 3 is 3-methylhexane; 2-ethylpentane uses a shorter parent.

questions.stem: The ketone CH3CH2COCH3 is named
questions.explanation: A four-carbon chain with C=O at carbon 2 is butan-2-one.

questions.stem: The correct name of CH3CH(CH3)CH(CH3)CH2CH3 among the following is
questions.explanation: The longest chain has five carbons with methyl groups at carbons 2 and 3, giving 2,3-dimethylpentane.

questions.stem: When ethyl and methyl compete as prefixes on a hexane chain at carbons 3 and 4, the preferred name begins
questions.explanation: Substituents are cited alphabetically (ethyl before methyl) and the chain is numbered to give the first point of difference the lower set; 3-ethyl-4-methylhexane is correct.

questions.stem: Calling a straight five-carbon saturated chain 1-methylbutane is wrong because the parent must be
questions.explanation: The longest chain has five carbons, so the hydrocarbon is pentane, not a methyl-substituted butane.

questions.stem: Isomers are compounds that have the same molecular formula but differ in
options: the number of protons in carbon
questions.explanation: Isomers share a formula yet differ in how atoms are connected or arranged in space.

questions.stem: Chain isomerism arises from different
options: carbon skeletons of the same formula
questions.explanation: Chain isomers have the same formula but different branching of the carbon chain.

questions.stem: Position isomerism is shown when compounds of the same formula differ in the
options: location of a functional group or multiple bond
questions.explanation: Position isomers have the same carbon skeleton and functional group type, but the group sits at different carbons.

questions.stem: Functional isomerism occurs when two compounds of the same formula have
questions.explanation: Functional isomers have the same molecular formula but belong to different classes (for example alcohol and ether).

questions.stem: Metamerism is isomerism in which alkyl groups on either side of a divalent function
options: differ, giving the same molecular formula
questions.explanation: Metamers differ in the alkyl groups attached to a divalent group such as —O— or —CO—.

questions.stem: Tautomerism is a special isomerism in which isomers exist in
questions.explanation: Tautomers, such as keto and enol forms, interconvert readily by a proton shift.

questions.stem: n-Butane and 2-methylpropane illustrate
questions.explanation: Both are C4H10; they differ only in whether the carbon chain is straight or branched.

questions.stem: Pentan-1-ol and pentan-2-ol are a pair of
questions.explanation: The hydroxy group is at carbon 1 in one and carbon 2 in the other, so they are position isomers.

questions.stem: Ethanol and methoxymethane are classic
questions.explanation: Both are C2H6O; one is an alcohol and the other an ether.

questions.stem: The saturated hydrocarbon C4H10 exists as how many chain isomers?
questions.explanation: C4H10 has n-butane and 2-methylpropane only.

questions.stem: The keto and enol forms of a carbonyl compound are
questions.explanation: Keto-enol pairs are tautomers in dynamic equilibrium.

questions.stem: Structural isomers differ from each other in the
questions.explanation: In structural (constitutional) isomerism the atoms are linked in different orders.

questions.stem: CH3CH2OCH2CH3 and CH3OCH2CH2CH3 are a pair of
questions.explanation: Both are C4H10O ethers that differ in the alkyl groups on either side of oxygen.

questions.stem: Pentane, 2-methylbutane and 2,2-dimethylpropane together show that C5H12 has
questions.explanation: Those three alkanes are the complete set of chain isomers of C5H12.

questions.stem: Propanal and propanone share the formula C3H6O and are therefore
questions.explanation: An aldehyde and a ketone of the same formula are functional isomers.

questions.stem: Which pair shows metamerism rather than tautomerism?
questions.explanation: The two ethers differ in alkyl groups about oxygen (metamers). The carbonyl-enol pairs are tautomers.

questions.stem: Tautomerism typically requires a mobile hydrogen together with a
questions.explanation: A proton shift and a shift of a double bond convert one tautomer into the other.

questions.stem: 1-Chlorobutane and 2-chlorobutane differ by
questions.explanation: The same C4 skeleton bears Cl at carbon 1 or carbon 2, which is position isomerism.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a type of structural isomerism?
questions.explanation: Geometrical (cis-trans) isomerism is stereo isomerism, not structural isomerism.

questions.stem: The formula C2H6O can represent an alcohol and an ether; those two compounds are
questions.explanation: Ethanol and methoxymethane have the same formula but different functional groups.

questions.stem: Alcohols with the formula C4H10O include butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol and the two methylpropanols, so the number of alcoholic structural isomers is
questions.explanation: The four isomeric alcohols are butan-1-ol, butan-2-ol, 2-methylpropan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol.

questions.stem: CH3COCH3 and CH2=C(OH)CH3 are related as
questions.explanation: Propanone and its enol form interconvert by a proton shift; they are tautomers, not metamers.

questions.stem: Geometrical isomerism needs restricted rotation, most often about a
questions.explanation: The C=C bond cannot rotate freely, so different spatial arrangements can persist as cis and trans forms.

questions.stem: In the cis isomer of an alkene the similar groups lie
options: on opposite sides of the double bond
on the same side of the double bond
on the same carbon atom only
questions.explanation: Cis means the like groups are on the same side of the C=C plane.

questions.stem: Trans geometrical isomers have the similar groups
options: on opposite sides of the double bond
on the same side of the double bond
free to rotate into cis instantly
questions.explanation: Trans places the similar substituents across the double bond from each other.

questions.stem: But-2-ene is a familiar alkene that exhibits
questions.explanation: Each carbon of the C=C in but-2-ene carries two different groups, so cis and trans forms exist.

questions.stem: An alkene cannot show cis-trans isomerism if one carbon of the double bond has
options: a hydrogen and an alkyl group
questions.explanation: If either doubly bonded carbon has two the same substituents, cis and trans are not distinct.

questions.stem: Cis-trans isomers belong to the broader class of
questions.explanation: Geometrical isomers have the same connectivity but different spatial arrangement, so they are stereoisomers.

questions.stem: Which alkene can show geometrical isomerism?
questions.explanation: In but-2-ene each C of the double bond has H and CH3; propene and 2-methylpropene have two identical groups on one carbon.

questions.stem: Restricted rotation about a C=C bond allows cis-trans forms provided each doubly bonded carbon is attached to
questions.explanation: Both carbons of the double bond must carry two unlike substituents for geometrical isomers to exist.

questions.stem: A 1,2-disubstituted cycloalkane can show cis-trans isomerism because the ring
options: prevents easy rotation about ring bonds
questions.explanation: The cyclic framework holds substituents on the same face (cis) or opposite faces (trans).

questions.stem: But-2-ene has two geometrical isomers while 2-methylpropene has none because in 2-methylpropene
options: one alkene carbon carries two methyl groups
questions.explanation: The (CH3)2C= end has two identical methyl groups, so cis and trans cannot be defined; but-2-ene has unlike groups on both carbons.

questions.stem: Homolytic bond fission produces
questions.explanation: Each bonded atom takes one electron, giving two species with unpaired electrons.

questions.stem: Heterolytic bond fission produces
questions.explanation: Both bonding electrons stay with one atom, generating a cation and an anion.

questions.stem: In homolytic cleavage each atom of the breaking bond takes
questions.explanation: Equal sharing of the bonding pair is the definition of homolysis.

questions.stem: In heterolytic cleavage both electrons of the shared pair go to
questions.explanation: Unequal taking of the pair creates ions.

questions.stem: Nucleophiles are reagents that are
options: electron-rich and seek a positive centre
questions.explanation: A nucleophile donates an electron pair to an electron-poor atom.

questions.stem: Electrophiles are reagents that are
questions.explanation: An electrophile accepts an electron pair at an electron-poor site.

questions.stem: A free radical is a species that has
options: a complete octet and no unpaired electron
questions.explanation: The unpaired electron is the hallmark of a free radical.

questions.stem: The hydroxide ion OH- acts in organic reactions as a
questions.explanation: OH- has lone pairs and a negative charge, so it is a typical nucleophile.

questions.stem: Anhydrous AlCl3 used in aromatic substitution is a typical
questions.explanation: AlCl3 has an incomplete octet and accepts an electron pair, so it is electrophilic.

questions.stem: Homolytic fission is often shown with a fish-hook arrow that moves
questions.explanation: A single-barbed (fish-hook) arrow tracks one-electron movement in radical processes.

questions.stem: A carbocation is classified as an
questions.explanation: The positively charged, electron-deficient carbon seeks electrons, so it is electrophilic.

questions.stem: Ammonia behaves as a nucleophile because nitrogen has
questions.explanation: The lone pair on N can be donated to an electrophilic carbon.

questions.stem: Homolytic fission of a covalent bond is favoured by
options: a strongly polar solvent and ionic reagents
questions.explanation: UV light, heat or a non-polar medium encourages each atom to keep one electron.

questions.stem: Heterolytic fission is more likely in
options: the gas phase with UV only
a polar solvent that can solvate ions
questions.explanation: Polar solvents stabilise the ions formed when both electrons stay on one atom.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a nucleophile?
questions.explanation: BF3 is electron-deficient (Lewis acid) and is an electrophile, unlike the lone-pair donors listed.

questions.stem: Chlorine atoms produced during photohalogenation of methane are
questions.explanation: Cl• has seven valence electrons including one unpaired electron, so it is a radical.

questions.stem: Heterolytic cleavage of HBr places both bonding electrons on bromine, so the fragments are
questions.explanation: Bromine is more electronegative, so it takes the pair and becomes Br- while hydrogen becomes H+.

questions.stem: In the dark ionic addition of HBr to an alkene the attacking species on carbon is an electrophile, whereas chlorination of methane in sunlight proceeds through
questions.explanation: Photochemical halogenation is a radical chain; polar addition of HBr starts with electrophilic H+.

questions.stem: The inductive effect is the transmission of electron displacement through
questions.explanation: Inductive polarisation is relayed along a chain of sigma bonds.

questions.stem: Alkyl groups relative to hydrogen are said to show the
questions.explanation: Alkyl groups push electron density along sigma bonds and are +I groups.

questions.stem: The nitro group attached to a carbon chain shows a strong
questions.explanation: —NO2 withdraws electrons through sigma bonds and is strongly -I.

questions.stem: The inductive effect becomes weaker as the
options: bond becomes a double bond only
questions.explanation: Sigma-bond polarisation dies out after a few carbon atoms.

questions.stem: The electromeric effect is a temporary complete transfer of a shared pair of
options: pi electrons to one atom of a multiple bond
questions.explanation: Electromeric displacement is the full shift of a pi pair when a reagent approaches.

questions.stem: Unlike the inductive effect, the electromeric effect operates only in the
questions.explanation: Electromeric polarisation is temporary and is called into play by a reagent.

questions.stem: Among the halogens attached to carbon, fluorine shows a particularly strong
questions.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative halogen, so C—F is strongly -I.

questions.stem: The tert-butyl group has a stronger +I effect than methyl because it
options: contains more alkyl carbon pushing electron density
questions.explanation: More alkyl branching increases the electron-releasing inductive effect.

questions.stem: The inductive effect is described as a
options: complete transfer of a pi pair
questions.explanation: The slight permanent shift of sigma electrons towards the more electronegative atom is inductive.

questions.stem: A +E electromeric shift means the pi electrons move
options: away from the atom that the reagent attacks
towards the atom at which the reagent attacks
questions.explanation: In the +E effect the pi pair is transferred to the atom of the multiple bond where the attacking reagent attaches.

questions.stem: The usual order of -I effect among the halogens is
questions.explanation: Electronegativity falls F to I, so the electron-withdrawing inductive effect follows F > Cl > Br > I.

questions.stem: Which of the following groups is electron-releasing by the inductive effect?
questions.explanation: The methyl group is +I; nitro, cyano and fluoro are -I substituents.

questions.stem: Chloroacetic acid is a stronger acid than acetic acid mainly because chlorine
options: shows -I and stabilises the carboxylate anion
is a +E group in the acid only
questions.explanation: The -I effect of Cl withdraws electron density and stabilises CH2ClCOO- relative to CH3COO-.

questions.stem: A key distinction is that inductive polarisation is partial and permanent, whereas electromeric polarisation is
questions.explanation: Electromeric effect is a full transfer of a pi pair while the reagent is present; it vanishes when the reagent is removed.

questions.stem: The +I order among the following alkyl groups is
questions.explanation: More substituted alkyl groups are more electron-releasing: (CH3)3C- > (CH3)2CH- > CH3CH2- > CH3-.

questions.stem: Formic acid is stronger than acetic acid because the methyl group in acetic acid
options: shows -I and stabilises the anion more
shows +I and makes loss of H+ less favourable
creates a double bond in the carboxyl
questions.explanation: The +I methyl increases electron density on the O-H and on the carboxylate, so acetic acid is the weaker acid.

questions.stem: Resonance in an organic molecule is the delocalisation of
options: pi electrons (or lone pairs) over adjacent atoms
questions.explanation: Resonance describes spreading of pi electrons or lone pairs through a conjugated system.

questions.stem: The actual molecule is better represented by the resonance hybrid than by any single
questions.explanation: Canonical forms are imaginary; the hybrid is the real electron distribution.

questions.stem: The alternative Lewis drawings of a delocalised species are called
questions.explanation: Canonical or contributing structures differ only in electron placement, not in atom connectivity.

questions.stem: Benzene is described as a resonance hybrid of two main Kekule forms, which explains its
options: equal C-C bond lengths and extra stability
questions.explanation: Delocalisation makes all six C-C bonds equivalent and lowers the energy (resonance energy).

questions.stem: Hyperconjugation is often called no-bond resonance because it involves delocalisation of
options: C-H sigma electrons of an alpha carbon into an adjacent empty or pi orbital
questions.explanation: Adjacent C-H bonds can overlap with a vacant p orbital or a pi bond; the contributing form has no bond to that hydrogen.

questions.stem: Hyperconjugation requires at least one hydrogen on a carbon attached to an
questions.explanation: Alpha C-H bonds next to C=C, C≡C or a carbocation are the usual source of hyperconjugation.

questions.stem: An alkene is generally more stable when it has more hyperconjugative structures, which means more
options: alpha hydrogens on alkyl groups attached to the C=C
halogen atoms on the double bond
questions.explanation: More alkyl C-H bonds adjacent to the double bond give more hyperconjugative forms and greater stability.

questions.stem: The carboxylate anion is resonance-stabilised because the negative charge is
questions.explanation: The two C-O bonds of RCOO- become equivalent through resonance.

questions.stem: The extra stability of a resonance hybrid compared with the most stable canonical form is the
questions.explanation: Resonance energy measures how much delocalisation lowers the energy.

questions.stem: Phenoxide ion is more stable than ethoxide ion mainly because phenoxide is
questions.explanation: The negative charge on phenoxide is spread over the ring by resonance; ethoxide has no such delocalisation.

questions.stem: The allyl carbocation is unusually stable for a primary cation because it is
questions.explanation: The vacant p orbital conjugates with the C=C, spreading the positive charge over two carbons.

questions.stem: The usual stability order of alkyl carbocations is 3° > 2° > 1° mainly because of
options: decreasing +I and hyperconjugation as substitution falls
the absence of any electronic effect
questions.explanation: More alkyl groups supply +I and more alpha C-H hyperconjugation, so a tertiary cation is the most stable.

questions.stem: The methyl cation cannot be stabilised by hyperconjugation because it has
options: no carbon-hydrogen bond on an adjacent carbon
questions.explanation: CH3+ has no neighbouring carbon to provide C-H sigma delocalisation.

questions.stem: Resonance differs from tautomerism because canonical forms are not real isomers, whereas tautomers are
options: identical in connectivity and in hydrogen position
questions.explanation: Tautomers differ in the position of a hydrogen and a double bond and can be isolated in principle; resonance forms cannot.

questions.stem: Which species shows resonance delocalisation of a pi system?
questions.explanation: The nitro group is conjugated with the benzene ring; methane and ethane have no pi system to delocalise.

questions.stem: But-2-ene is more stable than but-1-ene largely because but-2-ene has
options: more hyperconjugative structures from two alkyl groups on the C=C
questions.explanation: An internal double bond is flanked by more alpha C-H bonds, so hyperconjugation is greater.

questions.stem: The tert-butyl carbocation is more stable than the isopropyl cation because tert-butyl has
questions.explanation: Nine C-H bonds on the three methyl groups can hyperconjugate with the empty p orbital; isopropyl has six such hydrogens.

questions.stem: The C-Cl bond in chloroethene is shorter and less reactive than in chloroethane because a chlorine lone pair
options: conjugates with the double bond, giving the C-Cl bond partial double-bond character
converts the molecule into an ionic salt
questions.explanation: Resonance of Cl lone pair into the C=C strengthens and shortens C-Cl and makes the halogen less labile.

questions.stem: In a substitution reaction an atom or group in a molecule is
options: replaced by another atom or group
removed to form a small molecule only
questions.explanation: Substitution swaps one atom or group for another, as in chlorination of methane.

questions.stem: An addition reaction is typical of unsaturated compounds because the reagent
options: replaces a hydrogen on an alkane
questions.explanation: The pi bond opens and two new sigma bonds form to the adding reagent.

questions.stem: Elimination creates unsaturation by the loss of
options: a small molecule from adjacent atoms
questions.explanation: Typical eliminations lose HX or H2O from neighbouring carbons and form a C=C bond.

questions.stem: A rearrangement reaction is one in which
options: the molecular formula always changes by CH2
a group or the carbon skeleton migrates within the molecule
questions.explanation: Atoms are reorganised to a new connectivity, as in a 1,2-shift to a carbocation.

questions.stem: Hydrogenation of ethene to ethane is classified as
questions.explanation: H2 adds across the double bond, so the reaction is addition.

questions.stem: Chlorination of methane in sunlight is a typical
questions.explanation: A hydrogen of methane is replaced by chlorine.

questions.stem: Dehydrohalogenation of an alkyl halide with alcoholic KOH is
questions.explanation: Loss of HX from the alkyl halide produces an alkene.

questions.stem: Hydration of ethene to ethanol in acid is an example of
questions.explanation: Water adds across the C=C bond of ethene.

questions.stem: Aqueous KOH with bromoethane mainly gives substitution, whereas alcoholic KOH favours
questions.explanation: Hot alcoholic KOH promotes dehydrohalogenation; aqueous KOH promotes nucleophilic substitution to the alcohol.

questions.stem: The reaction of ethene with bromine water, which decolourises the bromine, is
questions.explanation: Br2 adds across the double bond to give a vicinal dibromide.

questions.stem: Nitration of benzene with mixed acid replaces a ring hydrogen by NO2, so the reaction type is
options: addition to a C=C of benzene
questions.explanation: Aromatic substitution keeps the ring intact while swapping H for the electrophile NO2+.

questions.stem: Pinacol converting to pinacolone is cited in Intermediate texts as a
questions.explanation: A methyl group migrates as the diol dehydrates, which is a rearrangement.

questions.stem: When 2-bromopropane is heated with alcoholic KOH the dominant organic product arises by
questions.explanation: Alcoholic KOH favours loss of HBr from the secondary halide, giving propene rather than the alcohol.

questions.stem: Aqueous silver nitrate with a tertiary alkyl halide can give an alcohol by substitution, while the same halide with strong bulky base tends to give an alkene; the two competing types are
questions.explanation: The carbocation (or concerted path) may be captured by water (substitution) or lose a proton (elimination).

questions.stem: Crystallisation is used to purify a solid that can be obtained from a
questions.explanation: The impure solid is dissolved in a suitable hot solvent and the pure compound crystallises on cooling.

questions.stem: Simple distillation separates liquids that differ sufficiently in
questions.explanation: The more volatile liquid distils first when boiling points are well apart.

questions.stem: Fractional distillation is preferred when two liquids have
options: identical boiling points and form no mixture
questions.explanation: A fractionating column gives many vaporisation-condensation cycles needed for close-boiling liquids.

questions.stem: Steam distillation is useful for organic liquids that are steam-volatile and
options: completely miscible with water in all proportions as azeotropes only
questions.explanation: The mixture boils below 100 °C when the compound and water are immiscible, carrying the organic vapour with steam.

questions.stem: Sublimation can purify a solid such as camphor or naphthalene because the solid
options: passes directly into vapour and back to solid
questions.explanation: The impurity that does not sublime is left behind.

questions.stem: Chromatography separates mixture components mainly by differences in
options: adsorption (or partition) on a stationary phase
questions.explanation: Components move at different rates because they adsorb or dissolve to different extents.

questions.stem: In column chromatography the mixture is usually placed on a packed column of
questions.explanation: Alumina or silica gel is a common adsorbent; a solvent elutes the components at different rates.

questions.stem: Thin layer chromatography uses a thin coating of adsorbent on
options: a glass, plastic or metal plate
questions.explanation: TLC is a quick adsorption chromatographic method on a coated plate.

questions.stem: Paper chromatography uses paper as the
options: stationary phase (with water in the fibres)
questions.explanation: Water held in cellulose is the stationary phase; the solvent is the mobile phase.

questions.stem: Differential extraction of an organic compound from water uses a
options: separating funnel and an immiscible organic solvent
questions.explanation: The solute distributes into the organic layer, which is then separated in a funnel.

questions.stem: Aniline is commonly purified by steam distillation because it is
options: an ionic salt insoluble in steam
steam-volatile and practically immiscible with water
questions.explanation: Steam carries aniline vapour at a temperature below its normal boiling point.

questions.stem: Crude petroleum is separated into useful fractions by
options: paper chromatography of the whole oil
questions.explanation: The large boiling-point range of petroleum is exploited in a fractionating column.

questions.stem: A mixture of two solids in which only one sublimes is best separated by
questions.explanation: The sublimable component is vaporised and condensed as a pure solid.

questions.stem: The Rf value in chromatography is the ratio of the distance travelled by the
options: solvent to the distance travelled by the solute
solute to the distance travelled by the solvent
questions.explanation: Rf = (distance moved by the spot) / (distance moved by the solvent front).

questions.stem: Simple distillation rather than fractional distillation is adequate when the two liquids have
options: boiling points only a few degrees apart
identical vapour pressures at all temperatures
questions.explanation: A large boiling-point gap lets the more volatile liquid distil without a long column.

questions.stem: o-Nitrophenol can be separated from p-nitrophenol by steam distillation because intramolecular hydrogen bonding makes the ortho isomer
options: more steam-volatile than the para isomer
completely miscible with water as a salt
questions.explanation: Intramolecular H-bonding in o-nitrophenol reduces intermolecular association, so it is carried by steam; p-nitrophenol hydrogen-bonds intermolecularly and is less volatile.

questions.stem: The Lassaigne test for nitrogen, sulphur and halogen in an organic compound begins with
options: boiling with concentrated nitric acid only
ignition in a Liebig tube only
questions.explanation: Sodium fusion converts covalently bound N, S and X into ionic sodium salts that can be tested in water.

questions.stem: A positive Lassaigne test for nitrogen is the appearance of
options: a white fumes of NH3 only
questions.explanation: NaCN from the fusion gives ferrocyanide, which with Fe3+ yields Prussian blue.

questions.stem: Sulphur in the sodium extract is indicated by a violet colour with
questions.explanation: Na2S and sodium nitroprusside form a violet complex.

questions.stem: Chlorine in Lassaigne's extract gives with acidified silver nitrate a
questions.explanation: AgCl is white (and soluble in dilute NH4OH).

questions.stem: Bromine in the sodium-fusion extract gives with AgNO3 a
questions.explanation: AgBr is pale yellow and only sparingly soluble in ammonia.

questions.stem: Iodine in Lassaigne's test is confirmed by a
questions.explanation: AgI is yellow and insoluble in ammonium hydroxide.

questions.stem: For nitrogen, the sodium extract is boiled with ferrous sulphate and then acidified with
options: ferric chloride (or an oxidising acid treatment)
questions.explanation: Fe2+ forms hexacyanoferrate(II); Fe3+ then produces Prussian blue.

questions.stem: The Prussian blue formed in the nitrogen test is essentially
questions.explanation: The blue pigment is Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3 (ferric ferrocyanide).

questions.stem: When nitrogen and sulphur are both present, the sodium extract with ferric chloride often gives a blood-red colour due to
questions.explanation: Sodium thiocyanate forms blood-red Fe(SCN)3 with Fe3+.

questions.stem: Metallic sodium is used in Lassaigne fusion because it converts covalently bound N, S and halogen into
options: water-soluble ionic salts such as NaCN, Na2S and NaX
questions.explanation: Ionic sodium salts dissolve in water and then give characteristic ionic tests.

questions.stem: Lassaigne's sodium-fusion test is not the method used to detect
options: the carbon-hydrogen skeleton by Prussian blue
questions.explanation: Carbon and hydrogen are shown by combustion (lime-water / anhydrous copper sulphate), not by the Prussian-blue nitrogen test.

questions.stem: If an organic compound contains both nitrogen and sulphur, extra care is needed in the nitrogen test because thiocyanate may form instead of cyanide; a reliable extra observation is the
options: blood-red colour with FeCl3 from NaSCN
violet iodine-starch in the extract without fusion
questions.explanation: NaSCN gives blood red with FeCl3. If only cyanide is wanted for Prussian blue, the extract is boiled with FeSO4 and Fe3+ under the usual nitrogen procedure, sometimes after decomposing thiocyanate.

questions.stem: Carbon and hydrogen in an organic compound are estimated by Liebig's method, in which the sample is
options: combusted and the CO2 and H2O weighed
titrated with AgNO3 in the cold
questions.explanation: C is converted to CO2 and H to H2O, which are absorbed and weighed.

questions.stem: In Dumas' method nitrogen of the organic compound is estimated as
questions.explanation: The sample is heated with CuO; nitrogen is collected as N2 and its volume is measured.

questions.stem: Kjeldahl's method converts organic nitrogen into
questions.explanation: Heating with concentrated H2SO4 gives (NH4)2SO4; alkali liberates NH3 which is estimated.

questions.stem: Carius method is used for the quantitative estimation of
options: only oxygen by direct weighing of O2
questions.explanation: The compound is heated with fuming HNO3 (and AgNO3 for halogen) in a sealed tube.

questions.stem: Oxygen in a typical Intermediate analysis is obtained
options: by a direct Carius weighing of O2
by difference after C, H, N, X and S are known
questions.explanation: There is no routine school-level direct oxygen estimation; its percentage is 100 minus the other elements.

questions.stem: Kjeldahl's method is not reliable for compounds in which nitrogen is present as a
options: amino acid that forms ammonium sulphate
questions.explanation: Nitro, azo and many heterocyclic nitrogens are not converted quantitatively to ammonium sulphate under the usual Kjeldahl digestion.

questions.stem: In Liebig combustion, carbon dioxide is absorbed in a strong alkali such as KOH, while water is absorbed in
options: anhydrous calcium chloride (or similar drying agent)
concentrated HNO3 in a Carius tube
questions.explanation: H2O is taken up by a drying agent and CO2 by KOH; the mass gains give %H and %C.

questions.stem: In the Carius estimation of chlorine the halogen is finally weighed as
options: AgCl precipitated in the sealed-tube procedure
questions.explanation: Fuming nitric acid oxidises the compound; chloride is precipitated as AgCl, whose mass gives %Cl.
